stem: If \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF\) and \(\angle A = 48^\circ\), then \(\angle D =\) ______.
solution: In similar triangles, corresponding angles are equal. Here \(\angle A\) and \(\angle D\) are corresponding angles, so \(\angle D = \angle A = 48^\circ\).

subtopic: Tangent and Secant to a Circle
stem: AP is a tangent at A drawn to the circle with centre O from an external point P. \(OP = 12\) cm and \(\angle OPA = 30^\circ\), then the radius of the circle is ______.
solution: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so \(\angle OAP = 90^\circ\). In right triangle OAP, \(\sin(\angle OPA) = \dfrac{OA}{OP}\), i.e. \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{r}{12}\). Hence \(r = 12 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 6\) cm.

stem: Seg AB is parallel to X-axis and co-ordinates of the point A are \((1, 3)\), then the co-ordinates of the point B can be ______.
solution: If seg AB is parallel to the X-axis, then A and B have the same y-coordinate. Since A is \((1, 3)\), the y-coordinate of B must be \(3\). Among the options only \((-5, 3)\) has y-coordinate \(3\).

stem: The value of \(2\tan 45^\circ - 2\sin 30^\circ\) is ______.
solution: \(2\tan 45^\circ - 2\sin 30^\circ = 2(1) - 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - 1 = 1.\)

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle ABC = 90^\circ\), \(\angle BAC = \angle BCA = 45^\circ\). If \(AC = 9\sqrt{2}\), then find the value of AB.
solution: Since \(\angle BAC = \angle BCA = 45^\circ\), \(\triangle ABC\) is an isosceles right-angled triangle with \(AB = BC\). By Pythagoras theorem, \(AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = 2AB^2\). So \((9\sqrt{2})^2 = 2AB^2 \Rightarrow 162 = 2AB^2 \Rightarrow AB^2 = 81 \Rightarrow AB = 9.\)
figureNote: Right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle marked at B; page 1.

stem: Chord AB and chord CD of a circle with centre O are congruent. If \(m(\text{arc } AB) = 120^\circ\), then find the \(m(\text{arc } CD)\).
solution: Congruent chords of a circle correspond to congruent (equal-measure) arcs. Therefore \(m(\text{arc } CD) = m(\text{arc } AB) = 120^\circ.\)

stem: Find the Y-co-ordinate of the centroid of a triangle whose vertices are \((4, -3)\), \((7, 5)\) and \((-2, 1)\).
solution: The Y-coordinate of the centroid \(= \dfrac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3} = \dfrac{-3 + 5 + 1}{3} = \dfrac{3}{3} = 1.\)

stem: If \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta\), then what will be the measure of angle \(\theta\)?
solution: \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta \Rightarrow \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = 1 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ.\)

stem: In the figure, seg AC and seg BD intersect each other at point P. If \(\dfrac{AP}{CP} = \dfrac{BP}{DP}\), then complete the following activity to prove \(\triangle ABP \sim \triangle CDP\).
solution: In \(\triangle APB\) and \(\triangle CPD\): \(\dfrac{AP}{CP} = \dfrac{BP}{DP}\) ... (given); \(\angle APB \equiv \angle CPD\) ... (vertically opposite angles). Therefore \(\triangle ABP \sim \triangle CDP\) ... (SAS test of similarity).
figureNote: Seg AC and seg BD intersecting at point P forming two triangles ABP and CDP; page 1.

stem: In the figure, \(\square ABCD\) is a rectangle. If \(AB = 5\), \(AC = 13\), then complete the following activity to find BC.
solution: \(\triangle ABC\) is a right-angled triangle (angle B \(= 90^\circ\)). By Pythagoras theorem, \(AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2 \Rightarrow 25 + BC^2 = 169 \Rightarrow BC^2 = 144 \Rightarrow BC = 12.\)
figureNote: Rectangle ABCD with diagonal AC drawn; page 2.

stem: Complete the following activity to prove: \(\cot\theta + \tan\theta = \operatorname{cosec}\theta \times \sec\theta\).
solution: L.H.S. \(= \cot\theta + \tan\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta \times \cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta \times \cos\theta}\) (since \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\)) \(= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} \times \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \operatorname{cosec}\theta \times \sec\theta =\) R.H.S.

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: If \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\), \(AB : PQ = 4 : 5\) and \(A(\triangle PQR) = 125\) cm\(^2\), then find \(A(\triangle ABC)\).
solution: For similar triangles, the ratio of areas equals the ratio of the squares of corresponding sides: \(\dfrac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \left(\dfrac{AB}{PQ}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{16}{25}.\) So \(A(\triangle ABC) = 125 \times \dfrac{16}{25} = 80\) cm\(^2\).

subtopic: Tangent and Secant to a Circle
stem: In the figure, \(m(\text{arc } DXE) = 105^\circ\), \(m(\text{arc } AYC) = 47^\circ\), then find the measure of \(\angle DBE\).
solution: B is an external point and BD, BE are secants. The measure of the angle between two secants from an external point equals half the difference of the intercepted arcs: \(\angle DBE = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } DXE) - m(\text{arc } AYC)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}(105^\circ - 47^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2}(58^\circ) = 29^\circ.\)
figureNote: Two secants from external point B cutting the circle; arcs DXE and AYC marked; page 2.

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle of radius 3.2 cm and centre 'O'. Take any point P on it. Draw a tangent to the circle through point P using the centre of the circle.
solution: Construction steps: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.2 cm. (2) Take any point P on the circle. (3) Draw ray OP (the radius). (4) At point P, construct a line perpendicular to OP (i.e. \(\angle OPT = 90^\circ\)). This perpendicular line through P is the required tangent, since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

stem: If \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{11}{61}\), then find the value of \(\cos\theta\) using trigonometric identity.
solution: Using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\): \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta = 1 - \left(\dfrac{11}{61}\right)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{121}{3721} = \dfrac{3600}{3721}.\) Therefore \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{60}{61}.\)

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(AB = 9\) cm, \(BC = 40\) cm, \(AC = 41\) cm. State whether \(\triangle ABC\) is a right-angled triangle or not? Write reason.
solution: Check: \(AB^2 + BC^2 = 9^2 + 40^2 = 81 + 1600 = 1681\) and \(AC^2 = 41^2 = 1681.\) Since \(AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2\), by the converse of Pythagoras theorem \(\triangle ABC\) is a right-angled triangle, with the right angle at B.

stem: In the figure, chord PQ and chord RS intersect each other at point T. If \(\angle STQ = 58^\circ\) and \(\angle PSR = 24^\circ\), then complete the following activity to verify: \(\angle STQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } PR) + m(\text{arc } SQ)\right]\).
solution: In \(\triangle PTS\), by the exterior angle theorem \(\angle SPQ = \angle STQ - \angle PSR = 58^\circ - 24^\circ = 34^\circ.\) By the inscribed angle theorem, \(m(\text{arc } QS) = 2 \times \angle SPQ = 2 \times 34^\circ = 68^\circ.\) Similarly \(m(\text{arc } PR) = 2\angle PSR = 2 \times 24^\circ = 48^\circ.\) Therefore \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } QS) + m(\text{arc } PR)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}(68^\circ + 48^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2}(116^\circ) = 58^\circ\) ...(I). But \(\angle STQ = 58^\circ\) ...(II) given. From (I) and (II), \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } PR) + m(\text{arc } QS)\right] = \angle STQ.\)
figureNote: Circle with chords PQ and RS intersecting at interior point T; page 2.

stem: Complete the following activity to find the co-ordinates of point P which divides seg AB in the ratio \(3 : 1\) where \(A(4, -3)\) and \(B(8, 5)\).
solution: By the section formula, \(x = \dfrac{m x_2 + n x_1}{m + n}\), \(y = \dfrac{m y_2 + n y_1}{m + n}\) with \(m : n = 3 : 1\). So \(x = \dfrac{3 \times 8 + 1 \times 4}{3 + 1} = \dfrac{24 + 4}{4} = \dfrac{28}{4} = 7\) and \(y = \dfrac{3 \times 5 + 1 \times (-3)}{3 + 1} = \dfrac{15 - 3}{4} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3.\) Therefore \(P = (7, 3).\)

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), seg XY \(\parallel\) side AC. If \(2AX = 3BX\) and \(XY = 9\), then find the value of AC.
solution: Since \(XY \parallel AC\), \(\triangle BXY \sim \triangle BAC\) (AA test), so \(\dfrac{XY}{AC} = \dfrac{BX}{BA}\). From \(2AX = 3BX\) we get \(AX = \dfrac{3}{2}BX\), so \(BA = BX + AX = BX + \dfrac{3}{2}BX = \dfrac{5}{2}BX\), giving \(\dfrac{BX}{BA} = \dfrac{2}{5}.\) Hence \(\dfrac{9}{AC} = \dfrac{2}{5} \Rightarrow AC = \dfrac{45}{2} = 22.5.\)
figureNote: Triangle ABC with segment XY parallel to side AC, X on AB and Y on BC; page 3.

stem: Prove that, "Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary".
solution: Let \(\square ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in a circle. By the inscribed angle theorem, an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. So \(\angle B = \dfrac{1}{2}\,m(\text{arc } ADC)\) and \(\angle D = \dfrac{1}{2}\,m(\text{arc } ABC)\). Adding, \(\angle B + \angle D = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } ADC) + m(\text{arc } ABC)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}(360^\circ) = 180^\circ.\) Similarly \(\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ.\) Hence opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

stem: \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\). In \(\triangle ABC\), \(AB = 5.4\) cm, \(BC = 4.2\) cm, \(AC = 6.0\) cm, \(AB : PQ = 3 : 2\), then construct \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle PQR\).
solution: Since \(AB : PQ = 3 : 2\), the sides of \(\triangle PQR\) are \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) of the corresponding sides of \(\triangle ABC\): \(PQ = \dfrac{2}{3}(5.4) = 3.6\) cm, \(QR = \dfrac{2}{3}(4.2) = 2.8\) cm, \(PR = \dfrac{2}{3}(6.0) = 4.0\) cm. Construction: (1) Construct \(\triangle ABC\) with \(AB = 5.4\), \(BC = 4.2\), \(AC = 6.0\) cm. (2) Draw ray BX making an acute angle with BC. (3) Mark 3 equal points \(B_1, B_2, B_3\) on BX; join \(B_3\) to C. (4) Through \(B_2\) draw a line parallel to \(B_3C\) meeting BC at Q'. (5) Through Q' draw a line parallel to AC to get the scaled triangle; then construct \(\triangle PQR\) with \(PQ = 3.6\), \(QR = 2.8\), \(PR = 4.0\) cm.

stem: Show that: \(\dfrac{\tan A}{\left(1 + \tan^2 A\right)^2} + \dfrac{\cot A}{\left(1 + \cot^2 A\right)^2} = \sin A \times \cos A.\)
solution: Using \(1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A\) and \(1 + \cot^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A\): \(\dfrac{\tan A}{(\sec^2 A)^2} = \tan A \cdot \cos^4 A = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}\cos^4 A = \sin A\cos^3 A.\) Similarly \(\dfrac{\cot A}{(\operatorname{cosec}^2 A)^2} = \cot A \cdot \sin^4 A = \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}\sin^4 A = \cos A\sin^3 A.\) Adding, \(\sin A\cos^3 A + \cos A\sin^3 A = \sin A\cos A(\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A) = \sin A\cos A \times 1 = \sin A \times \cos A.\)

stem: \(\square ABCD\) is a parallelogram. Point P is the midpoint of side CD. Seg BP intersects diagonal AC at point X, then prove that: \(3AX = 2AC\).
solution: In parallelogram ABCD, \(AB \parallel DC\) and \(AB = DC\). Since P is the midpoint of CD, \(PC = \dfrac{1}{2}DC = \dfrac{1}{2}AB\), so \(AB = 2\,PC\). In \(\triangle AXB\) and \(\triangle CXP\): \(AB \parallel PC\) gives \(\angle XAB = \angle XCP\) and \(\angle XBA = \angle XPC\) (alternate angles), so \(\triangle AXB \sim \triangle CXP\) (AA test). Therefore \(\dfrac{AX}{CX} = \dfrac{AB}{PC} = \dfrac{2\,PC}{PC} = 2\), i.e. \(AX = 2CX\). Now \(AC = AX + XC = AX + \dfrac{1}{2}AX = \dfrac{3}{2}AX\). Hence \(2AC = 3AX\), i.e. \(3AX = 2AC.\)
figureNote: Parallelogram ABCD with P midpoint of CD, diagonal AC and seg BP intersecting at X; page 3.

stem: In the figure, seg AB and seg AD are tangent segments drawn to a circle with centre C from exterior point A, then prove that: \(\angle A = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } BYD) - m(\text{arc } BXD)\right]\).
solution: B and D are the points of contact of the tangents from A, so \(CB \perp AB\) and \(CD \perp AD\), giving \(\angle ABC = \angle ADC = 90^\circ\). In quadrilateral ABCD, \(\angle A + \angle ABC + \angle BCD + \angle ADC = 360^\circ\), so \(\angle A + \angle BCD = 360^\circ - 180^\circ = 180^\circ\), i.e. \(\angle A = 180^\circ - \angle BCD.\) Now \(\angle BCD\) is the central angle of arc BXD, so \(m(\text{arc } BXD) = \angle BCD\), and \(m(\text{arc } BYD) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc } BXD)\). Then \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } BYD) - m(\text{arc } BXD)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[(360^\circ - m(\text{arc } BXD)) - m(\text{arc } BXD)\right] = 180^\circ - m(\text{arc } BXD) = 180^\circ - \angle BCD = \angle A.\) Hence \(\angle A = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc } BYD) - m(\text{arc } BXD)\right].\)
figureNote: Two tangent segments AB and AD from external point A to a circle with centre C; arcs BYD (far) and BXD (near) marked; page 3.

stem: Find the co-ordinates of centroid of a triangle if points \(D(-7, 6)\), \(E(8, 5)\) and \(F(2, -2)\) are the mid-points of the sides of that triangle.
solution: The centroid of a triangle coincides with the centroid of the triangle formed by the midpoints of its sides (the medial triangle). So the required centroid \(= \left(\dfrac{-7 + 8 + 2}{3}, \dfrac{6 + 5 - 2}{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{3}{3}, \dfrac{9}{3}\right) = (1, 3).\)

stem: If a and b are natural numbers and \(a > b\). If \((a^2 + b^2)\), \((a^2 - b^2)\) and \(2ab\) are the sides of the triangle, then prove that the triangle is right angled. Find out two Pythagorean triplets by taking suitable values of a and b.
solution: The largest side is \((a^2 + b^2)\). Consider \((a^2 - b^2)^2 + (2ab)^2 = a^4 - 2a^2b^2 + b^4 + 4a^2b^2 = a^4 + 2a^2b^2 + b^4 = (a^2 + b^2)^2.\) Since the square of the largest side equals the sum of squares of the other two sides, by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the triangle is right-angled. Examples: for \(a = 2, b = 1\): sides \(a^2 - b^2 = 3\), \(2ab = 4\), \(a^2 + b^2 = 5\) giving the triplet \((3, 4, 5)\); for \(a = 3, b = 2\): sides \(a^2 - b^2 = 5\), \(2ab = 12\), \(a^2 + b^2 = 13\) giving the triplet \((5, 12, 13)\).

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Construct two concentric circles with centre O with radii 3 cm and 5 cm. Construct a tangent to the smaller circle from any point A on the larger circle. Measure and write the length of the tangent segment. Calculate the length of the tangent segment using Pythagoras theorem.
solution: Construction: (1) Draw two concentric circles with centre O of radii 3 cm and 5 cm. (2) Take any point A on the larger circle; join OA (\(= 5\) cm). (3) Draw the perpendicular bisector of OA to get its midpoint M. (4) With centre M and radius MO, draw an arc cutting the smaller circle at point B. (5) Draw line AB; it is the required tangent to the smaller circle (touching at B). Since OB \(\perp\) AB (radius \(\perp\) tangent), in right triangle OBA, \(AB = \sqrt{OA^2 - OB^2} = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\) cm. So the tangent segment measures 4 cm.
